questions.prompt:
The Glossary manager wants to boost the basket value and reduce missed cross-sell opportunities. The manager believes that certain items, such as milk, bread, cheese, butter, eggs, bananas, and coffee, are frequently bought together; these items should be co-located on the shelves. For this scenario, apply the Apriori algorithm to verify that buying patterns are interesting to the users.

Consider the following transaction logs shown in Table Q.1A.

| TID | Items |
|---|---|
| T1 | milk, bread, egg |
| T2 | milk, bread, banana |
| T3 | milk, cheese, banana |
| T4 | bread, butter, cheese |
| T5 | milk, bread, butter, cheese |
| T6 | milk, coffee, bread |
| T7 | banana, cheese |
| T8 | milk, bread, egg, butter |
| T9 | milk, bread, cheese |
| T10 | coffee, bread |

Answer the followings (candidate set represented as C, Frequent itemset represented as L):

i. Build C₁ → L₁, C₂ → L₂, C₃ → L₃ with min support count = 4; list pruned candidates at each stage.

ii. Generate rules from the largest Lk with min_conf = 70%; compute support, confidence. If min_sup changes to 5, which itemsets drop? Briefly explain via the Apriori property.
questions.answer:
C1 counts: milk = 7; bread = 8; cheese = 5; butter = 3; egg = 2; banana = 3; coffee = 2.

L1 = {milk, bread, cheese}. C2 counts: bread+milk = 6; bread+cheese = 3; cheese+milk = 3. L2 = {{bread, milk}}. C3 and L3 are empty.

| Rule | Support (%) | Confidence (%) |
|---|---|---|
| milk → bread | 60 | 85.714286 |
| bread → milk | 60 | 75 |

Both rules pass. At minimum support count 5, no previously frequent itemset drops.
questions.explanation:
At the first stage, remove butter, egg, banana, and coffee because their counts are below 4. Generate the three pairs from the surviving singletons. Prune {bread, cheese} and {milk, cheese}, each with count 3; only {bread, milk}, with count 6, survives.

There are not two distinct frequent pairs to join into a 3-itemset, so the standard Apriori join creates no C3 candidate. Equivalently, the potential triple {bread, cheese, milk} is eliminated before counting because it contains infrequent pairs. Its count would be 2, but it is not a candidate that needs scanning.

The largest frequent itemsets have size 2. Rule support is 6/10 = 60% in either direction. Confidence is 6/7 for milk → bread and 6/8 for bread → milk. Both exceed 70%.

Raising the threshold to 5 retains the singleton counts 7, 8, 5 and the pair count 6. Thus none drops in this particular dataset. The Apriori property says every subset of a frequent itemset is frequent, and no superset of an infrequent itemset can become frequent. Support and confidence qualify the rules here; they do not by themselves prove causal or incremental purchasing effects.

questions.prompt: A medical equipment company claims that its new blood test kit has an average accuracy rate of 95%. A quality inspector believes the true accuracy may be different from the claimed value (it could be higher or lower). To verify the claim, a random sample of 36 test kits is taken, and the sample shows an average accuracy of 94.7% with a known population standard deviation of 0.02. At the 5% significance level, test whether the company's claim is justified. (critical z-values are ±1.96)
questions.answer:
Assuming the standard deviation 0.02 is on the proportion scale: z = -0.9. Fail to reject the claim at the stated significance level.

If 0.02 instead means percentage points, z = -90 and the claim is rejected; the paper does not specify that unit.
questions.explanation:
Set H0: μ = 0.95 and H1: μ ≠ 0.95. Convert the sample mean to 0.947 and use known σ = 0.02 on the same proportion scale. Then SE = 0.02/sqrt(36) = 0.003333333 and z = (0.947 - 0.95)/SE = -0.9. Since -1.96 < -0.9 < 1.96, the sample does not provide sufficient evidence that the true mean differs from the claim. Failure to reject does not prove the claimed accuracy.

Unit caveat: if σ were 0.02 percentage points instead of 0.02 proportion units, consistent percentage arithmetic gives (94.7 - 95)/(0.02/6) = -90. The two interpretations cannot be mixed.

questions.prompt: An ice cream manufacturer noticed that sales of ice cream increase every summer and drop in winter. The sales pattern repeats each year with increasing average sales overtime due to marketing efforts. Which components are present in this time series? Identify the time series model that would best represent this pattern and why?
questions.answer: The described components are an upward trend and annual seasonality. Use a trend-plus-seasonal model. An additive model is suitable if seasonal changes have roughly constant size; a multiplicative model is suitable if seasonal swings grow in proportion to the sales level.
questions.explanation: The increasing yearly average is trend; the recurring summer rise and winter fall are seasonal. A seasonal Holt-Winters model can represent both. The description does not state whether seasonal amplitude is constant or proportional to level, so it does not uniquely select additive versus multiplicative seasonality. An additive representation is Y = T + S + I; a multiplicative representation is Y = T × S × I. Neither a business-cycle component nor a specific irregular pattern is established by the description.

questions.prompt:
Table Q. 2A shown below has the data collected during the outbreak of smallpox.

| Group | Attacked | Not attacked | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vaccinated | 31 | 469 | 500 |
| Not Vaccinated | 185 | 1315 | 1500 |
| Total | 216 | 1784 | 2000 |

Test the effectiveness of vaccination in preventing smallpox at 5% significance level.
questions.answer:
Pearson chi-square = 14.643193; df = 1. Reject independence at 5%.

Vaccinated attack rate = 6.2%; unvaccinated attack rate = 12.333333%. Vaccination is associated with a lower attack rate in this sample.
questions.explanation:
Set H0: vaccination status and attack status are independent; H1: they are associated. Expected counts are row total × column total / 2000: vaccinated [54, 446] and unvaccinated [162, 1338]. They all exceed 5.

Compute χ² = (31-54)²/54 + (469-446)²/446 + (185-162)²/162 + (1315-1338)²/1338 = 14.643193, with (2-1)(2-1) = 1 degree of freedom. This exceeds the 5% critical value approximately 3.841, so reject H0. No continuity correction is used.

The attack proportions are 31/500 and 185/1500. Their direction supports effectiveness in the sense of a lower observed incidence among vaccinated people. Without randomization or control of confounding, this association alone is not a definitive causal estimate.

questions.prompt:
Consider frequent 1-itemsets:

L₁ = {A, B, C, D, E, F}.

Use the hash function

$h(x,y) = ((order(x) × 5) + order(y)) \bmod 7$

and the following transactions:

- T₁: {A, B, C}
- T₂: {A, D, E}
- T₃: {B, C, E, F}
- T₄: {A, B, E, F}.

i. Construct the hash table H₂ showing bucket addresses, counts, and contents.

ii. If the minimum support is 4, which buckets can be pruned?
questions.answer:
Using order(A)=1, …, order(F)=6 and x before y alphabetically:

| Bucket | Count | Contents with multiplicity |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 3 | AB × 2, CF × 1 |
| 1 | 3 | AC × 1, BE × 2 |
| 2 | 3 | AD × 1, BF × 2 |
| 3 | 4 | AE × 2, EF × 2 |
| 4 | 2 | DE × 1, AF × 1 |
| 5 | 0 | none |
| 6 | 3 | BC × 2, CE × 1 |

Prune buckets 0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6. Only bucket 3 survives the bucket-count filter.
questions.explanation:
Enumerate unordered pairs within each transaction, always placing the earlier letter first. T1 contributes AB, AC, BC; T2 contributes AD, AE, DE; T3 contributes BC, BE, BF, CE, CF, EF; T4 contributes AB, AE, AF, BE, BF, EF. There are 18 pair occurrences in total.

For example, h(A,B)=(1×5+2) mod 7=0 and h(A,E)=(1×5+5) mod 7=3. Count every occurrence, including repeats across transactions. A bucket below 4 cannot contain a pair with support count 4. However, a surviving bucket does not prove its pairs are frequent: AE and EF each occur only twice, and collisions give their shared bucket a count of 4. Consequently, there is no actually frequent pair at support 4. The paper calls all six singletons frequent even though their counts in these four logs are below 4; treat the supplied L1 as an instruction for the hashing exercise.

questions.prompt:
Two forecasting models for production planning are evaluated as follows:

| Model | MAE | MSE | RMSE | MAPE |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Model A | 12 | 25 | 5 | 6% |
| Model B | 10 | 36 | 6 | 4% |

Justify and explain which model gives better overall forecasting performance? Explain, considering all measures.
questions.answer: Taken at face value, B is better on MAE and MAPE; A is better on MSE and RMSE. There is no unconditional winner without a loss priority. More fundamentally, the reported table is inconsistent if each row uses the same forecast errors: RMSE cannot be smaller than MAE.
questions.explanation:
Lower errors are preferable. B has smaller typical absolute and percentage error, while A's smaller squared-error measures would favor it when large misses are especially costly. MSE and RMSE encode the same ranking, so counting four metrics as four independent votes is inappropriate.

For any common error sample, sqrt(mean(e²)) ≥ mean(|e|). Yet A reports 5 < 12 and B reports 6 < 10. Their MSE/RMSE pairs are internally consistent, but their MAE values cannot come from the same errors and scale. Verify the metric definitions, units, or source data before making an operational choice; do not silently correct the printed values.

questions.prompt:
i. Find the standard deviation and skewness for the following data:

78, 91, 68, 54, 82, 47, 60, 78, 97, 58, 62, 50, 50, 63, 92, 75 79, 63, 42, 61

ii. Give example for "Combining variables" concept in dataset preparation.

iii. A CMO of a company marketing carbonated soft drinks has developed three new flavors of cola and decided to measure the customers' preference for these three flavors from 12 customers by using scale of 1 to 9. The table of data is shown below. Conduct the appropriate analysis here.

| Flavor-A | Flavor-B | Flavor-C |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | 6 | 8 |
| 2 | 4 | 6 |
| 4 | 5 | 8 |
| 2 | 5 | 6 |
questions.answer:
i. Treating the printed '75 79' as two observations:

- Sample SD = 15.839657.
- Adjusted Fisher-Pearson sample skewness = 0.299970, mildly right-skewed.
- If population conventions are intended instead: population SD = 15.438588 and moment skewness = 0.276986.

ii. Combine quantity and unit price into total sales = quantity × unit price.

iii. Assuming three independent groups of four customers, one-way ANOVA gives F = 14.4 with numerator df = 2 and denominator df = 9. At an explicitly assumed 5% level, reject equal mean preferences. Mean ratings are A = 3, B = 5, C = 7.
questions.explanation:
i. The paper omits a comma between 75 and 79. Interpreting them as separate values gives n=20, sum=1350, mean=67.5, and squared deviations summing to 4767. Sample variance is 4767/19, so sample SD is 15.839657. With s denoting that sample SD, adjusted sample skewness is n/((n-1)(n-2)) × Σ((x-mean)/s)³ = 0.299970. The unadjusted moment coefficient uses m3/m2^(3/2)=0.276986. The question does not specify a skewness definition or sample/population convention; those choices must be stated. Pearson's median coefficient is a different definition and is not interchangeable with these moment coefficients.

ii. A derived sales variable combines two existing columns, quantity and unit price, into one quantity useful for aggregation.

iii. The table contains 12 ratings, four per flavor. Assuming they represent different customers, H0: μA=μB=μC. The grand mean is 5; between-group SS=4[(3-5)²+(5-5)²+(7-5)²]=32. Within-group SS=4+2+4=10. Thus MSB=32/2=16 and MSW=10/9; F=16/(10/9)=14.4. At 5%, the F(2,9) critical value is about 4.256, so at least one mean differs. Flavor C has the highest sample mean, but an overall ANOVA alone does not prove all pairwise differences. The significance level and independence are assumptions because the paper does not state them explicitly. If the same customers rated each flavor, a repeated-measures analysis would be required instead.

questions.prompt:
A dataset contains 100 transactions.

- 20 transactions include both {Pen, Notebook}.
- 25 transactions include {Pen}.
- 40 transactions include {Notebook}.

i. Calculate Support and Confidence for the rule {Pen} → {Notebook}.

ii. If the minimum support is 10% and minimum confidence is 60%, check whether the rule is strong.

iii. Interpret the result.
questions.answer: Support = 20%; confidence = 80%. The rule is strong under the stated thresholds.
questions.explanation: Support is count(Pen ∩ Notebook)/N = 20/100 = 20%. Confidence is count(Pen ∩ Notebook)/count(Pen) = 20/25 = 80%. Both 20% ≥ 10% and 80% ≥ 60%, so the rule passes. One fifth of all transactions contain both items, and four fifths of pen transactions also contain a notebook. This is a purchasing association, not proof that buying a pen causes a notebook purchase.

questions.prompt:
Consider the sales for the past 5 weeks: 120, 130, 125, 140, 150.

i. Compute the 3-week Simple Moving Average (SMA) forecast for week 6.

ii. Comment briefly on the difference between the SMA and WMA forecasts.
questions.answer: SMA forecast for week 6 = 138.333333 units. SMA weights the three observations equally; WMA can give more weight to recent observations. No numerical WMA is determined because weights are not given.
questions.explanation: Use the three most recent actual values, weeks 3–5: (125+140+150)/3 = 415/3. A weighted moving average instead uses weights summing to 1. If larger weights are placed on the more recent, larger observations here, its forecast would be higher and respond faster to the rise. The paper does not specify those weights, so a unique WMA value must not be invented.

questions.prompt:
Given the following transaction database:

| TID | Items |
|---|---|
| 1 | A, C |
| 2 | A, B, D |
| 3 | A, B, C |
| 4 | B, C, D |
| 5 | A, C |

a) Convert the above database into vertical data format and find all frequent itemsets with a minimum support of 2.

b) List the advantages of using vertical data format over horizontal format in frequent itemset mining?
questions.answer:
Vertical representation:

| Item | TID set | Support count |
|---|---|---|
| A | {1, 2, 3, 5} | 4 |
| B | {2, 3, 4} | 3 |
| C | {1, 3, 4, 5} | 4 |
| D | {2, 4} | 2 |

Frequent pairs:

| Itemset | TID set | Support count |
|---|---|---|
| AB | {2, 3} | 2 |
| AC | {1, 3, 5} | 3 |
| BC | {3, 4} | 2 |
| BD | {2, 4} | 2 |

All four singletons and these four pairs are frequent. No itemset of size three or larger is frequent.
questions.explanation:
Intersect singleton TID sets to obtain pair support. The excluded pairs AD and CD each have count 1. The only triple whose pairs all survive is ABC, with intersection {3} and count 1; it also fails. Thus there are 8 nonempty frequent itemsets in total.

Vertical mining calculates support by TID-set intersections instead of rescanning every horizontal transaction for each candidate. It can reuse intersections, prune low-support branches, and use bitsets or compressed lists for efficient operations. TID storage can still be large, so these advantages do not imply that vertical format always uses less memory.

questions.prompt:
A supermarket's market-basket analysis generates several association rules, such as:

- Rule 1: Diapers → Beer (support = 5%, confidence = 80%)
- Rule 2: Milk → Bread (support = 20%, confidence = 60%)

Some rules may appear strong based on support and confidence but can be misleading.

a. Explain why some association rules can be misleading even if they have high support and confidence.

b. Identify at least two additional measures that can be used to evaluate the true strength of a rule.
questions.answer: High confidence can arise simply because the consequent is common. High support can likewise reflect popular items rather than a meaningful dependence. Additional measures include lift, Kulczynski, and cosine.
questions.explanation:
Lift compares P(B|A) with P(B): lift=P(A∩B)/(P(A)P(B)). Lift above, equal to, or below 1 indicates positive association, independence, or negative association in this probabilistic sense. Kulczynski averages both directional confidences: 0.5[P(B|A)+P(A|B)]. Cosine is P(A∩B)/sqrt(P(A)P(B)). The latter two are null-invariant and assess co-occurrence from complementary perspectives.

Neither example provides the individual item supports needed for these calculations, so the rules cannot be ranked reliably from their support and confidence alone. No association measure proves causation.

questions.prompt:
A transportation company tracks its monthly passenger counts (Yt). The data for the first five months are given. Applying Holt's Method

| Period | Month | Passenger Count |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Jan | 400 |
| 2 | Feb | 450 |
| 3 | Mar | 520 |
| 4 | Apr | 500 |
| 5 | May | 550 |

Parameters: Use smoothing constants

a. Calculate the initial Level (L1) and Trend (T2).

b. Calculate the final Level (L5) and Trend (T5) based on all five data points.

c. Use L5 and T5 to provide the forecast for Month 7 (F7).
questions.answer:
Initial level = 400; initial trend = 50 passengers per month, using the first difference.

L5, T5, and F7 are not uniquely determined: the printed paper omits both smoothing constants. Once they are supplied, the month-7 forecast is F7 = L5 + 2T5.
questions.explanation:
The source says 'Parameters: Use smoothing constants' but shows no numerical α or β. It also calls the initial trend T2; under the usual first-difference initialization it is Y2−Y1=450−400=50. To make indexing explicit, initialize L1=400 and T1=50, then update from t=2. This yields L2=450 and T2=50, so the requested initial T2 is also 50 under this convention.

For supplied constants, use L(t)=αY(t)+(1−α)[L(t−1)+T(t−1)] and T(t)=β[L(t)−L(t−1)]+(1−β)T(t−1). After the February update, the remaining symbolic steps are:

- L3=α(520)+(1−α)(450+50), and T3=β(L3−450)+(1−β)50.
- L4=α(500)+(1−α)(L3+T3), and T4=β(L4−L3)+(1−β)T3.
- L5=α(550)+(1−α)(L4+T4), and T5=β(L5−L4)+(1−β)T4.
- Month 7 is two periods after month 5, so F7=L5+2T5.

These are the complete computable steps from the supplied information. Assigning numerical smoothing constants would create a different problem.

questions.prompt:
An online electronics store analysed 1,000 customer purchase transactions. The following data were obtained:

| Itemset | Number of Transactions |
|---|---|
| {Smartphone} | 420 |
| {Wireless Earbuds} | 380 |
| {Smartphone, Wireless Earbuds} | 260 |

(a) Calculate the pattern evaluation measures such as Lift, Kulc and cosine for the following association rule:

Smartphone → WirelessEarbuds

(b) Justify the relationship between Smartphone and Earbud purchases based on the obtained Lift and Kulc values.
questions.answer:
Lift = 1.629073; Kulc = 0.651629; cosine = 0.650814.

The items co-occur more often than independence would predict. Kulc is the average of the two directional confidences, approximately 65.16%.
questions.explanation:
Let A be Smartphone and B be Wireless Earbuds. P(A)=420/1000=0.42, P(B)=380/1000=0.38, and P(A∩B)=260/1000=0.26.

Lift=0.26/(0.42×0.38)=1.629073. The observed joint support is about 1.63 times the independent expectation, showing positive association. Kulc=0.5(260/420+260/380)=0.651629. Cosine=260/sqrt(420×380)=0.650814.

The conditional proportions are approximately 61.90% and 68.42%; Kulc balances those directions. A Kulc value alone has no universal independence threshold analogous to lift=1, and these purchasing associations do not establish causality.

questions.prompt:
A data analyst is studying the annual income levels (in ₹000s) of 12 employees in a company:

[180, 200, 210, 215, 220, 230, 250, 270, 300, 320, 400, 480]

Apply both equal-width and equal-frequency binning with 3 bins.

Using histogram analysis, discuss which binning approach (equal-width or equal-frequency) provides a better representation of the income distribution and justify your reasoning.
questions.answer:
Equal-width bin width = 100 (₹000s).

| Equal-width interval | Values | Count |
|---|---|---|
| [180, 280) | 180, 200, 210, 215, 220, 230, 250, 270 | 8 |
| [280, 380) | 300, 320 | 2 |
| [380, 480] | 400, 480 | 2 |

| Equal-frequency bin | Values | Count |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 180, 200, 210, 215 | 4 |
| 2 | 220, 230, 250, 270 | 4 |
| 3 | 300, 320, 400, 480 | 4 |

Equal-width bins more directly show the concentration at lower incomes and the sparse upper tail. Equal-frequency bins are useful for balanced groups but hide that concentration if only equal bar heights are shown.
questions.explanation:
Width=(480−180)/3=100. Use left-closed/right-open intervals except that the final interval includes the maximum. This produces counts 8, 2, 2. Equal-frequency binning sorts the 12 values and places the first four, next four, and final four together.

For displaying the distribution's shape, equal-width bars permit direct frequency comparisons over the same income span. Equal-frequency bins have differing widths; an honest histogram must use frequency density, count divided by width, so area rather than height represents frequency. Equal-frequency grouping is not intrinsically wrong, but raw counts alone make every group look equally common despite very different income spans.
